posts.title: Four o’clock sound check
posts.excerpt: At four the lawn is empty, the lanterns are still folded and the only audience is a sound engineer with one ear free of the headphones.
posts.content:
At four in the afternoon the Harbour Lawn belongs to the crew. The gates are still shut, the lanterns hang unlit and the stage is a floor of cables and tape marks. Daniel Osei, who mixes the sound from a desk in the middle of the grass, walks the lawn first, clapping once at each corner to hear what the harbour does with it.

The sound check is short by design. Each act gets ten minutes, one song and the chance to say what they hear in their own monitors. The piano is tuned the night before and again at noon, because salt air and a hot afternoon never agree. The brushes and the double bass are the hardest to balance, so they go first.

By half past four the engineer has a rough picture of the evening: where the wind will carry the horns, how much of the water to leave in the quiet songs. The first brass notes at 16:30 then arrive on a lawn that has already been listened to once.

posts.title: How six hundred lanterns go up
posts.excerpt: Paolo Conti’s team starts at noon with a rope line, a short ladder and a list of six hundred numbers nobody has ever lost.
posts.content:
The lanterns go up on the day, never before. At noon Paolo Conti and his crew run rope lines between the lighting masts and the quay rail, then hang the lanterns in strings of twenty. Every string is checked against a list, and every lantern is lifted by hand, because the paper is thin and the harbour wind is not.

Lighting them is the part the audience sees. At 20:40 a crew member on a short ladder walks each line, one lantern at a time, and the lawn warms from the stage outwards. It takes about fifteen minutes, which is why the schedule marks it as a row of its own and not as part of a set.

At 01:00 the crew takes them down again, string by string, and counts them back into their crates. Six hundred go out, six hundred come back, and the paper is reused until it tears.

posts.title: Coming by boat
posts.excerpt: The shuttle from Old Town Pier takes twelve minutes and leaves every twenty. It is also the best first view of the lawn.
posts.content:
The easiest way to reach Saltmere Quay is on the water. A boat leaves Old Town Pier every twenty minutes from 15:00 and crosses the harbour in twelve. From the deck the lawn comes into view as a dark green patch with a stage at one end, and after sunset it comes into view as a field of lanterns.

The last boat back leaves the quay at 23:40 on Saturday and 22:40 on Sunday. A return ticket is €9 and can be added to any festival ticket when you request it. Tram line 4 also stops at Saltmere Quay, and there are bike racks for 300 at Gate B.

Whichever way you come, bring a blanket. The lawn is soft, the evenings are cool by the water and about four hundred low chairs are available to borrow at Gate A.
